name: Pitcairn Island

pin.note: Approximate centre of Pitcairn Island, near Adamstown (25°04′S 130°06′W)

territory: Pitcairn, Henderson, Ducie and Oeno Islands - a British Overseas Territory (United Kingdom)

creatures.iucn_status: Endangered (uplisted from Vulnerable in 2008; Vulnerable D1+2 proposed in the 2026.1 Red List update, not yet confirmed as final)
creatures.status_note: Endemic to Pitcairn Island, estimated at about 1,568 birds in 2022/23; recent work suggests a stable population but a very small range.

facts.statement: Pitcairn Island is centred at roughly 25.07 degrees south, 130.11 degrees west (25°04′S, 130°06′W) in the South Pacific.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox coordinates.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn lies in the isolated south-central Pacific, about 2,170 km southeast of Tahiti.
facts.evidence_note: Opening summary gives the distance and direction from Tahiti.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is the only inhabited island of its territory, and the UNESCO listing places it about 200 km southwest of uninhabited Henderson Island.
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Site description states Pitcairn lies roughly 200 km to the southwest of Henderson.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pitcairn group has four islands (Pitcairn, Henderson, Ducie and Oeno) with about 47 km2 of land in total, of which Henderson accounts for about 86%.
facts.evidence_note: Territory overview and area figures.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn lies just south of the Tropic of Capricorn and is warm all year; one source gives an average temperature range of 19-24 °C.
facts.evidence_note: Climate line in infobox/section plus territory page note on the Tropic of Capricorn.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Adamstown's climate is classed as tropical rainforest (Köppen Af) with no dry season; February is warmest (mean 23.8 °C) and August coolest (mean 18.5 °C).
facts.evidence_note: Climate section and its table.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Wikipedia's climate table gives annual rainfall on Pitcairn of about 1,543 mm, spread fairly evenly through the year, with southeast trade winds moderating the climate; a UNEP-WCMC Henderson Island document puts the mean at probably 1,300 to 1,500 mm.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section; the territory article independently gives about 1,540 mm. Re-checked 2026-10-09: no primary source confirmed it. Wikipedia gives 1,543 mm (1972-2004 table), but the only authoritative source I opened (Henderson Island WCMC doc) says the mean is probably 1,300-1,500 mm, and no official meteorological source was found.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pacific Union College Pitcairn Islands Study Center reports average rainfall near 2,000 mm, with 2,170 mm measured on Pitcairn in 1991/92, and monthly mean temperatures from about 24 °C (January) to 19 °C (July).
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Islands Study Center: wetlands and environment
facts.publisher: Pacific Union College Pitcairn Islands Study Center
facts.evidence_note: Climate paragraph of the environment page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Recorded extremes at Pitcairn include a high of 33.3 °C in March, and temperatures have not fallen below 10 °C; tropical cyclones are a hazard mainly from November to May.
facts.evidence_note: Climate and hazards sections.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is a volcanic island with a rugged cliff-lined coast and no protective coral reefs around it.
facts.evidence_note: Geology/terrain description in the article. Re-checked 2026-10-09: no primary source confirmed it. Wikipedia says volcanic origin, rugged cliff coastline and no protective coral reefs; the Cambridge paper confirms only 'small volcanic island' and no authoritative page on the reefs was opened.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The highest point is the Pawala Valley Ridge, given as 346 m above sea level by one source and 347 m by another.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox elevation (346 m); geography article gives 347 m.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is small: about 4.5 km2, roughly 3.5 km long and 1.8 km wide according to one source (others give 5 km2 or 450 ha).
facts.evidence_note: Infobox area and dimensions.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A steep road known as the Hill of Difficulty climbs from Bounty Bay, the mutineers' landing place, up to the Edge, according to the Pitcairn Government.
facts.evidence_note: Settlement description; the Pitcairn Island article also notes the Bounty Bay pier as sole access. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Government of the Pitcairn Islands; the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. Pitcairn Government page confirms the Hill of Difficulty road from Bounty Bay; gov.uk Overseas Territories information paper confirms Adamstown as only settlement; 'only landing is a small pier' was not confirmed (Wikipedia's Adamstown page itself does not say pier).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Within the group Pitcairn is volcanic, Henderson is an uplifted coral island, and Oeno and Ducie are coral atolls.
facts.evidence_note: Geology list of the four islands. Re-checked 2026-10-09: SPC describes Pitcairn as a dead volcano, Henderson as a raised fossilised coral atoll, and Oeno and Ducie as coral atolls.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Polynesians settled Pitcairn and Henderson around the 11th century, and contact with other islands such as Mangareva faded by the mid-1400s; both islands were later found uninhabited.
facts.evidence_note: Early-history timeline entries.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Captain Philip Carteret's crew sighted Pitcairn on 3 July 1767, though his recorded longitude was about 3 degrees off.
facts.evidence_note: 1767 timeline entry. Re-checked 2026-10-09: no primary source confirmed it. Wikipedia gives 3 July 1767 and a roughly 3 degree longitude error; a hobbyist blog said 2 or 3 July and 3 degrees, and no authoritative source was opened.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Bounty mutineers settled Pitcairn in January 1790 with six Polynesian men, twelve Polynesian women and an infant girl, and the ship was burned on 23 January 1790, as reported by the Pitcairn Islands Study Center.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Islands Study Center history timeline
facts.publisher: Pacific Union College, Pitcairn Islands Study Center
facts.evidence_note: 1790 timeline entries. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Pacific Union College, Pitcairn Islands Study Center; the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. PUC confirms 23 Jan burning, 6 men, 12 women, baby girl but gives no exact arrival day (15 Jan only on Wikipedia); Pitcairn Government also says 1790 with 6 men, 12 women, an infant girl; 'Tahitians' is narrower than 'Polynesians'.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On 20 September 1793 violence killed most of the remaining English settlers, including Fletcher Christian; John Adams later became the community's leader.
facts.evidence_note: 1793 and 1800 timeline entries (attributed account).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 1814 visit by HMS Briton and HMS Tagus counted about 46 inhabitants on Pitcairn, according to the Naval Chronicle; one contemporary letter says 40.
facts.publisher: Naval Chronicle (period source, hosted by Univ. of Denver)
facts.evidence_note: 1808 and 1814 timeline entries. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Naval Chronicle (period source, hosted by Univ. of Denver); the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. Naval Chronicle says 'about 46 persons' but an earlier quoted letter says 40; Feb 1808 (6 Feb log entry) is from Pacific Union College's Pitcairn Study Center and the NSW library only confirms the year 1808.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In 1856 the Pitcairn community, reported as 194 people, sailed on the Morayshire on 3 May and reached Norfolk Island on 8 June; some families returned from 1859, according to the Pitcairn Islands Study Center.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Islands Study Center: History, Part 5
facts.publisher: Pitcairn Islands Study Center, Pacific Union College
facts.evidence_note: 1838 and 1856 timeline entries. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Pitcairn Islands Study Center, Pacific Union College; the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. The Study Center gives 194 people (not 163), arrival 8 June 1856 and returns in 1859, and does not mention the 30 Nov 1838 colony date.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn is a British Overseas Territory, the only one in the Pacific, under a 2010 constitution; the UK keeps responsibility for defence and foreign affairs.
facts.evidence_note: Territory status and government paragraphs. Re-checked 2026-10-09: no primary source confirmed it. Wikipedia matches; legislation.gov.uk confirms a Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 exists, but defence/foreign affairs division and 'only Pacific territory' could not be confirmed in any opened primary page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Local government is led by an elected Island Council that acts as the legislature, with a Mayor customarily heading day-to-day administration and a King's Governor appointed from the UK.
facts.evidence_note: Governor and government section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A UN Special Committee on Decolonization working paper gives Pitcairn's population as 42 people in 2022, including some who were temporarily away.
facts.publisher: United Nations Special Committee on Decolonization
facts.evidence_note: Population section; the Adamstown article also gives 35 for 2023. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against United Nations Special Committee on Decolonization; the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. UN paper lists 42 (2022) and no 233/1937 peak; Wikipedia's own table says 250 in 1936 and SPC says 233 in 1886, so the peak claim is internally inconsistent and should be dropped.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Native land animals on Pitcairn are insects and lizards, large numbers of seabirds nest on its steep shores, and humpback whales pass or breed in surrounding waters.
facts.evidence_note: Fauna paragraph; territory article mentions humpbacks breeding.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Of the territory's 20 breeding bird species, 16 breed on Henderson Island, which is also home to the flightless Henderson crake.
facts.evidence_note: Ecology paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island has four endemic land birds, ten endemic vascular plant taxa out of about 57 native, and roughly one-third of collected insects and snails are endemic; it is the only known breeding site of the Henderson petrel.
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Species/endemism paragraph of the inscription text.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn's waters hold at least 1,249 species of marine mammals, seabirds and fish, and the reserve includes a coralline alga living 382 m below the surface.
facts.source_title: Pew, National Geographic Applaud Creation of Pitcairn Islands Marine Reserve
facts.evidence_note: Species and ecosystem bullet points.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The plant Abutilon pitcairnense, once native to Pitcairn, is now extinct in the wild, and about 16 plant species are thought endemic to Pitcairn.
facts.evidence_note: Flora note; endemic count from the territory article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: UNESCO lists three threats on Henderson Island: invasive rats (Polynesian rat) that deplete bird populations, unguarded landings by visitors, and marine plastic debris washing ashore.
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Threats paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2011 poison-baiting campaign against Pacific rats on Henderson failed: 60-80 survivors out of an estimated 50,000-100,000 rats allowed full recovery.
facts.evidence_note: Rat eradication section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The UK government announced a marine reserve of about 834,334 km2 around the islands on 18 March 2015, monitored with satellite surveillance against illegal fishing.
facts.source_title: Pew, National Geographic Applaud Creation of Pitcairn Islands Marine Reserve
facts.evidence_note: Size, date and protections; Visit Pitcairn gives ~834,000 km2 and a September 2016 legal designation.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988 under natural criteria (vii) and (x).
facts.source_title: Henderson Island - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
facts.evidence_note: Inscription year and criteria fields.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pitcairn reed warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) is found only on Pitcairn Island; it was formally described by Sharpe in 1900 and locals call it the sparrow.
facts.evidence_note: Taxonomy and distribution sections. Re-checked 2026-10-09: no primary source confirmed it. A Cambridge Bird Conservation International paper confirms the species is confined to Pitcairn, but Sharpe 1900 and the 'sparrow' local name were only confirmed via Wikipedia.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: A 2024 peer-reviewed survey estimated about 1,568 Pitcairn reed warblers and recommended reclassifying the species from Endangered to Vulnerable, describing the Endangered listing as largely speculative.
facts.source_title: Population status of the endemic Pitcairn Reed Warbler Acrocephalus vaughani on Pitcairn Island, South Pacific (Oppel, Eisler and Aspey, 2024)
facts.evidence_note: Status section; the territory article also notes the 2008 listing. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Bird Conservation International (Cambridge University Press); the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. Peer-reviewed paper calls the Endangered status largely speculative with no earlier population assessments, contradicting the 'surveys showed it was rarer' rationale; the 2008 date is only on Wikipedia and BirdLife/IUCN pages could not be loaded.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: The Pitcairn reed warbler was found in all habitats surveyed on Pitcairn and appeared most abundant in stands of introduced rose apple (Syzygium jambos), according to a 2024 population survey.
facts.source_title: Population status of the endemic Pitcairn Reed Warbler Acrocephalus vaughani on Pitcairn Island, South Pacific
facts.evidence_note: Habitat paragraph; the Cambridge paper also reports highest abundance in rose apple. Re-checked 2026-10-09 against Bird Conservation International (Cambridge University Press); the statement keeps only the parts that source supports. The paper supports rose apple abundance but does not mention pandanus, bare ground, or 'generalist' in the summary I could read; BirdLife page failed to load.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: A 2022/23 survey estimated about 1,568 Pitcairn reed warblers (95% confidence interval 812-3,237).
facts.source_title: Population status of the endemic Pitcairn Reed Warbler Acrocephalus vaughani on Pitcairn Island, South Pacific
facts.evidence_note: Abstract population estimate.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: Of 49 monitored nests, only four failed to fledge young; productivity was 1.07 fledglings per nest, which the authors judge enough to maintain the population.
facts.source_title: Population status of the endemic Pitcairn Reed Warbler Acrocephalus vaughani on Pitcairn Island, South Pacific
facts.evidence_note: Abstract nest-monitoring results.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: The 2024 study's authors recommended downlisting the warbler from Endangered to Vulnerable, and a February 2026 Red List discussion proposed Vulnerable under criteria D1+2; final publication was pending.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Reed-warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) - 2026.1 Red List discussion
facts.evidence_note: Proposed status paragraph; Cambridge abstract gives the recommendation.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: Threats to the warbler include a possible arrival of other rat species or cats, past habitat loss, and some soil erosion; it currently coexists with Pacific rats.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Reed-warbler (Acrocephalus vaughani) - 2026.1 Red List discussion
facts.evidence_note: Threats list in the discussion thread.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: GBIF's backbone resolves Acrocephalus vaughani (Sharpe, 1900) as an accepted species in family Acrocephalidae with usage key 5231321.
facts.evidence_note: Exact species match result.
facts.subject: pitcairn-reed-warbler

facts.statement: The Henderson petrel (Pterodroma atrata), which Wikipedia lists as Endangered (IUCN 3.1), is believed to nest only on Henderson Island in the Pitcairn group; current colony numbers are put at about 40,000, and Brooke estimated roughly 16,000 breeding pairs in 1991/92.
facts.evidence_note: Status, population and breeding-site statements from the page text; the page notes Ducie colonies were lost to rats by 1922. Status is as shown on Wikipedia, not read from IUCN.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Henderson crake (Zapornia atra), a flightless rail found only on Henderson Island, is listed as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1) by Wikipedia, with about 5,600 mature individuals (range 3,800-8,400) as of 2022.
facts.evidence_note: Status and 2022 population estimate on the page; the page says numbers had recovered to pre-2011 levels by 2015. Status not read from IUCN directly.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Henderson fruit dove (Ptilinopus insularis) is endemic to Henderson Island and is listed as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1) by Wikipedia; its population is described as stable at roughly 3,000-4,000 mature individuals.
facts.evidence_note: Infobox status and population statement. Status not read from IUCN directly. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Stephen's (Henderson) lorikeet, Vini stepheni, is endemic to Henderson Island and is listed as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1) by Wikipedia, which gives a stable population of 720-1,820 individuals.
facts.evidence_note: Population and status in the page text. The page names the location inconsistently as Pitcairn Island in one place, but the rest of the article places the bird on Henderson, so Henderson is used. Status not read from IUCN directly. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Henderson reed warbler (Acrocephalus taiti) is endemic to Henderson Island, living in coastal coconut groves and scrub as well as undisturbed interior forest, and Wikipedia lists it as Vulnerable (IUCN 3.1) after a 2022 assessment.
facts.evidence_note: Habitat and status statements; the page gives no population figure. Status not read from IUCN directly.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Murphy's petrel (Pterodroma ultima) nests on rocky islets and cliffs of the Pitcairn, Austral and Tuamotu groups and is listed as Least Concern (IUCN 3.1) by Wikipedia; the Ducie Island page says more than 90% of the world's population breeds on Ducie.
facts.evidence_note: Status and habitat come from the Murphy's petrel page; the >90% Ducie figure comes from the Ducie Island article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ducie_Island). Two Wikipedia pages combined.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pacific Union College Pitcairn Islands Study Center lists seven waterbird species for the group, notes that the Bristle-thighed Curlew, a non-breeding visitor, is a threatened species, and says the Henderson Island Crake occurs only on Henderson.
facts.source_title: Pitcairn Islands Study Center: wetlands and environment
facts.publisher: Pacific Union College Pitcairn Islands Study Center
facts.evidence_note: Waterbird and species sections. Page gives no formal Red List category or year, so only the word 'threatened' is reported; the page is an older summary.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Endemic fishes named by the UK Government Marine Science blog as found only in the Pitcairn Islands include the Pitcairn sandlance, the Henderson triplefin and a squirrelfish species.
facts.source_title: In deep water: understanding the future climate risks to Pitcairn's coral reefs
facts.evidence_note: Biodiversity paragraph; no conservation status given and scientific names are not given on the page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cefas Blue Belt report card says Pitcairn Islands reefs have no recorded bleaching events, and that the 2012 expedition measured coral cover of 56% at Ducie, 28% at Oeno, 24% at Henderson and 5% at Pitcairn Island.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Sections on coral reefs and bleaching (pp. 3-5). Cover figures are from the 2012 expedition cited by the report.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A cold-water intrusion in 1970 caused mass coral mortality at Ducie, according to the Cefas Blue Belt report card; Wikipedia's Ducie page likewise attributes the largely dead lagoon coral to cold-water influxes.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Bleaching section (p. 5). Wikipedia Ducie Island article is consistent but is a separate source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Surface seawater around the Pitcairn Islands has a mean pH near 8.12 and aragonite saturation approaching 3.2; under a high-emissions scenario the Cefas report card projects surface pH to fall by 0.27 units by the end of the century.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Ocean acidification section (p. 6). Earlier estimates of 7.91-8.12 are also mentioned.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island's beaches hold the highest density of plastic debris reported anywhere in the world: a mean of 239.4 items/m2 and up to 671.6 items/m2 on the surface, with an estimated 37.7 million items weighing about 17.6 tons.
facts.source_title: Exceptional and rapid accumulation of anthropogenic debris on one of the world's most remote and pristine islands
facts.publisher: ADrift Lab (Lavers and Bond, PNAS 2017 abstract)
facts.evidence_note: Abstract figures; about 68% of beach debris was buried under 10 cm of sediment. The page's accumulation rate unit looks garbled and is omitted.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island has poor soil and little fresh water; its only known potable source is a brackish spring on the north shore, exposed at half tide and rising from a crevice in flat rock.
facts.evidence_note: Freshwater paragraph.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Pitcairn Island's domestic water comes mainly from rainwater harvested in tanks, but a 2010 SOPAC scoping mission found that long-term droughts had affected its 48 residents and that the island's only borehole and its springs had recently dried up.
facts.source_title: SOPAC conducts water scoping mission in Pitcairn Island
facts.evidence_note: Mission of 30 May to 10 June 2010; conditions describe that time and may have changed.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Ducie Atoll's lagoon is about 16 m deep at most, has a sand and coral bottom and a channel roughly 91 m wide, and drains through caves to the ocean, causing frequent whirlpools; it holds about 138 fish species.
facts.evidence_note: Coral and Lagoon section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Pitcairn Islands Marine Protected Area was established in 2016 and is given as 841,910 km2 by the Cefas report card, whereas Wikipedia and Pew give 834,334 km2 for the March 2015 reserve announcement.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: MPA area (p. 3). Conflict with figures already in the library; the sources do not reconcile the difference.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In the 1972-2004 climate table for Pitcairn Island, January is the driest month (96.5 mm) and December the wettest (157.7 mm), for an annual total of 1,542.7 mm, so rainfall is not completely even.
facts.evidence_note: Monthly table; the article text calls rain evenly distributed.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cefas reports three ocean heat events peaking in 1995, 2006 and 2017 that mainly affected Oeno, Pitcairn and Henderson, and notes the Pacific warm pool stretches toward Pitcairn in El Nino years.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Sea surface temperature section (p. 4).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cefas projects sea surface temperature around the Pitcairn Islands to rise by 0.5 C by 2050 and 0.9 C by 2099 under medium emissions, or by 2 C by 2050 and nearly 4 C by 2100 under high emissions.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Projections (p. 4).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Cefas report card says some sea-level rise rates reported in the western South Pacific are about four times the global average (approximately 12 mm a year), El Nino and La Nina shift levels by roughly 20-30 cm, and Pitcairn has no tide gauges so no accurate local record exists.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Sea level rise section (p. 8); the 12 mm figure is regional, not Pitcairn-specific. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Cefas judges long-distance ocean swells from remote low-pressure systems to be a greater risk to Pitcairn than a direct cyclone hit, and notes such swells are especially frequent in strong El Nino years.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Cyclones and extreme weather section (p. 10).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A record rainfall event on Pitcairn Island in 2012 caused landslides and sedimentation that contributed to some coral mortality, according to the Cefas report card.
facts.source_title: Climate change impacts on corals in BIOT and the Pitcairn Islands (Blue Belt report card)
facts.evidence_note: Storms section (p. 11).
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In a 2012 survey, grey reef sharks made up 46% of top-predator biomass across the Pitcairn Islands but were rare at Oeno and Pitcairn Island, which the authors link to fishing; 22 of 205 reef fish species (about 11%) were regional endemics.
facts.source_title: Friedlander et al. 2014, The state of the coral reef ecosystems of the Pitcairn Islands
facts.publisher: University of California Santa Barbara (hosted peer-reviewed paper)
facts.evidence_note: Results summary; fetched text was an automated summary of the paper.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 2012 Pitcairn Islands survey recorded 70 hard coral species and 64 macroalgal taxa, and found erect macroalgae covering about 42% of the seabed at Pitcairn Island, where coral cover was only about 5%.
facts.source_title: Friedlander et al. 2014, The state of the coral reef ecosystems of the Pitcairn Islands
facts.publisher: University of California Santa Barbara (hosted peer-reviewed paper)
facts.evidence_note: Results summary; fetched text was an automated summary of the paper.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Henderson Island has 51 native flowering plant species, ten of them endemic, and no native mammals; Pacific rats introduced by Polynesians about 800 years ago remain abundant.
facts.evidence_note: Vegetation and rats sections; UNESCO gives a different plant count (about 57 native vascular species), so sources differ.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Of the territory's 20 breeding bird species, Henderson has 16, Ducie 13, Oeno 12 and Pitcairn only 6, and all four islands are BirdLife Important Bird Areas.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife section.
facts.subject: island

Age and hotspot origin of Pitcairn's volcano not found
Pitcairn government (gov.pn) page unreachable; official sources limited to the tourism site
conflicts: Area of Pitcairn: 4.5 km2 (Wikipedia) vs 5 km2 (Geography article) vs 450 ha (PUC)
Highest point: 346 m vs 347 m vs 335 m (PUC)
Annual rainfall: ~1,800 mm vs ~1,540 mm vs ~2,000 mm (PUC)
Henderson distance from Pitcairn: ~200 km SW (UNESCO) vs 193 km NE (Wikipedia)
Polynesian departure: mid-1400s cut-off (History article) vs abandoned in the 17th or early 18th century (territory article)
